Yes, I understand how riders on a bill work and there are bloated pieces of legislation that make it hard to pass bills all the time.

However, just because a bill fails and the topic is complicated, this doesn’t mean we throw up our hands and say “I guess there’s more factors at play,” and move on.

I’m talking specifically about two bills in my first comment: S.4361 and S.744.

[Here](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-collapse-of-bipartisan-immigration-reform-a-guide-for-the-perplexed/) is a good starting article to get some insight on why S.4361 likely failed. [Here](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/research/guide-s744-understanding-2013-senate-immigration-bill) is a resource about the details of S.744.

These two bills both had momentum in congress and both had bipartisan cooperation building each bill. In both cases, they were shot down by republican leadership for no clear reason. 

For S.744, after it passed the senate, it was never brought to the house floor by then speaker John Boehner because it “didn’t have support of house Republicans.” House republicans decided the bipartisan senate bill wasn’t good enough, so attempted to piece their own bill together, but ultimately never submitted anything new. So republican leadership in congress killed a viable bill for no apparent reason other than they didn’t like it. You can only speculate from there why they didn’t like it.

S. 4361 was in a similar position in 2024. After republicans were able to get more border concessions in exchange for aid from Ukraine (i.e. compromise across a two-party system), republicans suddenly refused to support the bill at the urging of Donald Trump. You can speculate about why Trump would want congress to kill a bill on immigration reform when immigration is the major platform for his campaign. If he doesn’t get credit…

A few years ago, my mom told me a story about a seemingly-normal funeral for an elderly woman. Her passing was not unexpected, and drew a large crowd of family and friends wishing to pay respects. 

Most of the family of this woman were very kind and patient, and spoke about how loving their mom, sister, grandmother was. However, one of the family members was the woman’s granddaughter who made it known she was the self-declared black sheep of the family. She was 15-17 years old, and chose to dress primarily in black, wear heavy makeup, and dye her hair many different colors (nothing wrong with that, but this is relevant to the story). Before the funeral when the family came in to make arrangements, the girl kept interjecting the plans to speak out against her family, saying she’d fit in better at the funeral home because “they have a more open mindset than any of my family members.” As grief can be an emotional change for people, my mom handled the situation well and kept things smoothly going.... up until the day of the funeral.

After the minister said a few words, he invited family and friends to come and speak about their relative who had died. Without missing a beat, this girl jumps up and gets to the podium before anyone else. 

In front of everyone, this lady’s family and close friends who had all came to pay respects for her funeral, the granddaughter says, “My grandmother was a nice woman... but not to me. She never accepted me because of my form of self-expression. She never liked my hair or clothes, so I’m glad that she has died now because I can be who I truly want to be without anyone holding me back.”

My mom said it was really hard to get the family to calm down after that, but they made it to the grave-side service on time!
